summary: This RFC is the official specification of the format of the Internet host table, the file listing host names and addresses. It brings RFC 810 up to date with minor revisions.

eli5.summary: Before the phone book of names existed, everyone kept one big list of computer names and numbers. This tells how to write that list.

questions: what was the internet host table format
what characters are allowed in a host name
what does a hosts.txt entry look like
subtitle: The text-file format that listed every network, gateway and host name with its address, before DNS took over that job.

tldr.problem: Hosts on the DoD Internet needed one agreed way to list names and addresses of networks, gateways, hosts and domains so that the list could be shared and read by programs.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 952 defines a plain ASCII table where each entry has up to 6 colon-separated fields: a keyword (NET, GATEWAY, HOST or DOMAIN), addresses, names, machine type, operating system and protocols. It also gives the rules for legal names.
tldr.outcome: It is the official specification of the host table format, updating RFC 810. The unit metadata lists RFC 1123 as updating it.

facts.label: Address form
facts.value: Four decimal numbers, one octet each

today: RFC 952 is listed as updated by RFC 1123, and its status is not recorded as Standard or Historic in the metadata for this site. It replaced RFC 810 as the specification of the host table format.

sections.title: What the Host Table Is
sections.content:
RFC 952 is the official specification of the format of the Internet Host Table. It is a minor revision of RFC 810 that brings it up to date, and it lists RFC 810 and RFC 608 as obsoleted.

The table is used by the DoD Hostname Server, which the DDN Network Information Center (NIC) maintains on behalf of the Defense Communications Agency (see RFC 953). A machine-translatable ASCII version lived in the file NETINFO:HOSTS.TXT on the SRI-NIC host. It could be fetched by FTP (logging in as ANONYMOUS with password GUEST) or from the NIC Hostname Server, which the RFC calls the faster and easier route.

Users of the table are responsible for translating it into whatever format they need.
sections.eli5: Imagine one master address book for a whole school. This RFC says what the master book looks like and where to get a copy.

sections.title: Rules for Names
sections.content:
A name (of a net, host, gateway or domain) is a text string of up to 24 characters. The allowed characters are letters (A-Z), digits (0-9), the minus sign and the period. Periods are only allowed when they separate the components of a domain style name. Names have no blanks and are not case sensitive.

The first character must be a letter, and the last must not be a minus sign or period. Single-character names and nicknames are not allowed.

  • A host that works as a gateway should have -GATEWAY or -GW in its name; other hosts should not.
  • A DoD host that is a TAC should end its name with -TAC.

Names and addresses for DoD hosts and gateways are negotiated and registered with the DDN PMO and then the NIC before use. Domains and networks are registered with the DDN Network Information Center.
sections.eli5: Computer names follow spelling rules, like a school that says names must start with a letter and cannot have spaces. Gateways get a special tag in their names so people can spot them.

sections.title: Addresses in the Table
sections.content:
Internet addresses are 32 bits (see RFC 796). In the table each address is written as four decimal numbers separated by periods, and each number stands for one octet.

The first bits of the address decide how it splits into a network number and a local address (see RFC 943). A first bit of 0 gives a Class A address with a 7-bit net number. First bits 1,0 give Class B with a 14-bit net number, and 1,1,0 give Class C with a 21-bit net number. The local address identifies a host within the network.

The ARPANET (net 10) and MILNET (net 26) are both Class A networks. For these, the second octet identifies the physical host, the third the logical host, and the fourth the Packet Switching Node (PSN), formerly called an Interface Message Processor (IMP).
sections.eli5: An address is like a street number with parts: the first part says which neighborhood, the rest says which house. The first few digits tell you how big the neighborhood part is.

sections.title: Entry Format and Syntax
sections.content:
Each entry is an ASCII text string with up to 6 fields, separated by colons, and it ends with a colon. Fields 4 to 6 are optional.

  • Field 1: keyword NET, GATEWAY, HOST or DOMAIN.
  • Field 2: the address, followed by any alternate addresses (for a domain, the addresses where a Domain Name Server exists).
  • Field 3: the official name, with optional nicknames where permitted.
  • Field 4: machine type. Field 5: operating system. Field 6: protocol list.

A semicolon starts a comment. Commas separate data elements, and two colons in a row mark a null field. Protocol information is written TRANSPORT/SERVICE, for example TCP/TELNET, and either half may be given alone. Blanks and tabs are ignored between elements but not allowed inside one, and a line starting with a blank continues the previous one.

NET entries cannot have alternate addresses or nicknames, and DOMAIN entries do not use fields 4 to 6. Fields 3 to 6 describe the first address in field 2. Nicknames for hosts are discouraged except while old and new names are both kept during a rename. The table is grouped by type in the order Domain, Net, Gateway, Host, and the order within a type is unspecified.

The RFC also gives a parsing grammar and a lexical grammar for entries.
sections.eli5: Each line of the book is a row of boxes split by colons: what kind of thing it is, its number, its name, and then a few details. Some boxes can be left empty.

sections.title: Example Entries
sections.content:
The RFC shows four sample lines: two networks (ARPANET and PURDUE-CS-NET), a gateway named MIT-GW.ARPA with two addresses, the SRI-NIC host itself with a long protocol list, and a TAC named SU-TAC.ARPA.

Reading the SRI-NIC line: it is a HOST with addresses 26.0.0.73 and 10.0.0.51, official name SRI-NIC.ARPA with nicknames SRI-NIC and NIC, machine type DEC-2060, system TOPS20, and a list of protocols such as TCP/TELNET and TCP/FTP.
sections.eli5: The examples are sample rows from the address book, showing a network, a gateway and two computers filled in.

data.title: Example of host table format
data.code:
NET : 10.0.0.0 : ARPANET :
NET : 128.10.0.0 : PURDUE-CS-NET :
GATEWAY : 10.0.0.77, 18.10.0.4 : MIT-GW.ARPA,MIT-GATEWAY : PDP-11 :
          MOS : IP/GW,EGP :
HOST : 26.0.0.73, 10.0.0.51 : SRI-NIC.ARPA,SRI-NIC,NIC : DEC-2060 :
       TOPS20 :TCP/TELNET,TCP/SMTP,TCP/TIME,TCP/FTP,TCP/ECHO,ICMP :
HOST : 10.2.0.11 : SU-TAC.ARPA,SU-TAC : C/30 : TAC : TCP :
